Cache-Control Checker

Sends one real HTTP GET request to a URL you choose and classifies the response's caching headers into well-documented misconfiguration patterns: Vary: * (uncacheable by any compliant cache, ever), Cache-Control: public alongside a Set-Cookie header (a shared cache can leak one visitor's cookie to another), plus notices for contradictory or silently-ignored directive combinations and a static asset with no caching headers at all. Only point it at a system you own or are authorised to test.

Chasing a specific symptom? Why isn't my CDN caching this? walks the six response-header reasons a shared cache stores nothing, in the order worth checking them.

1. Run the CLI against your site

Node.js, no dependencies to install:

node check.mjs https://example.com --json

Get check.mjs, probe.mjs, and analyze.mjs from the repo — plain Node, nothing to install. It only ever talks to the URL you pass; nothing goes through this site.

2. Paste the JSON output here

Paste the JSON from step 1 and click Check.

Report

Raw caching headers

Common questions

Why does Vary: * make a response uncacheable forever?

RFC 9111 defines Vary: * as meaning this response varies on something a cache cannot inspect, so no cache -- browser or CDN -- may ever reuse a stored copy of it, for any later request, no matter how similar. It overrides Cache-Control and Expires entirely: they say a response is cacheable, Vary: * says it can never actually be served from that cache. It usually appears by accident, copied from a template or added defensively, rather than as a deliberate choice.

Why is Cache-Control: public with a Set-Cookie header dangerous?

public tells every shared cache between the server and the visitor -- a CDN edge, a corporate proxy -- that it may store this exact response and serve it to a different visitor. If the response also sets a cookie meant for the one visitor who received it (a session token, a CSRF token, a personalised value), a shared cache that is not specifically configured to strip Set-Cookie on write can hand visitor A's cookie to visitor B on the next request for that URL. This is a real, repeatedly-reported class of CDN misconfiguration, not a hypothetical.

If Cache-Control and Expires disagree, which one wins?

Cache-Control's max-age wins in any HTTP/1.1-or-later-compliant cache; Expires is kept only for the rare cache that predates HTTP/1.1. So if the two headers disagree -- a common drift when one is set by application code and the other by a proxy or CDN default -- only a legacy cache will ever notice, and even then it honours the older, usually-wrong value. Worth syncing the two or dropping Expires entirely rather than leaving them to drift apart.

Why flag a weak ETag on a response that supports byte-range requests?

RFC 9110 requires a strong validator to satisfy a conditional Range request -- a weak ETag (the W/ prefix) cannot be used to confirm a resource hasn't changed since an earlier partial fetch. A client resuming a download, or a media player seeking within a video or audio file, relies on exactly that guarantee. A weak ETag on such a response means range requests either fall back to fetching the whole file again or risk serving inconsistent bytes across a resumed transfer.

Does a clean report mean the site's caching is fully correct?

No. This checks a specific, well-documented set of caching-header patterns from one response -- it is not a full caching or performance audit, does not crawl other pages on the site, and cannot see a misconfiguration this tool's checks don't happen to cover (response security headers like CSP are out of scope here -- see security-headers-check for those). Treat a clean report as evidence about these specific patterns, not a determination that the site's caching strategy is optimal.

Evidence, not a determination. This checks a specific, well-documented set of caching-header patterns from one response. It is not a full caching or performance audit, does not crawl other pages on the site, and cannot see a pattern it doesn't check for. A clean report describes what this one request found, not a guarantee the site's caching strategy is optimal.

vs-checking-headers-by-eye-in-devtools.h.text:
← Cache-Control Checker

This checker vs. checking headers by eye in DevTools

Browser DevTools -- the Network tab's Headers panel -- shows the raw response headers for a request you've already made, for free, with nothing to install. It is a fine first look at what a server actually sent, and for a page you're already inspecting it is often the fastest option there is. What it does not do is tell you which of those headers, in combination, form a well-documented misconfiguration: a Vary: * that makes the whole response uncacheable forever, or a Cache-Control: public alongside a Set-Cookie header that lets a shared cache leak one visitor's cookie to the next. Reading raw headers in a panel and knowing what they mean together are two different skills.

This tool sends one request to a URL you name and classifies the response's caching headers into seven named, RFC-backed patterns, stating in plain English why each one matters and which header proves it. It does not replace DevTools -- for a page open in your browser right now, the Network tab is still the quickest way to glance at a response. It automates the reading a person would otherwise have to do by eye, every time, and it runs from a terminal or CI job where clicking through a Network tab isn't practical.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I have a page open in my browser and want a quick look at its response headers. DevTools' Network tab -- that quick raw look is exactly its job.
I want to know whether a response's caching headers have a named misconfiguration, and why it matters. This checker -- names the pattern (Vary: *, a public + Set-Cookie leak, and five more) instead of leaving you to notice it in a headers panel.
I want this checked automatically on every deploy, with a non-zero exit code on a real problem. This checker's CLI -- node check.mjs <url> --json exits non-zero on a danger-severity finding. DevTools has no CLI to wire into CI.
I'd rather not learn all seven RFC-backed patterns from memory to read a headers panel myself. This checker -- paste the CLI's JSON into the browser report and get the plain-English findings without already knowing the rules.

Neither tool replaces the other, and in practice most people use both: DevTools for a fast raw look at one response you're already looking at, this tool for the recurring, automatable question of whether that response's caching headers actually do what they look like they do.

Try it

node check.mjs https://example.com --json

One request to the URL you name, the same kind your browser already sends. Paste the JSON into the checker for the plain-English report.

Common questions

Should I use this tool instead of DevTools?

Different jobs, and most people who use this tool also still open DevTools. The Network tab's Headers panel shows you the raw response headers for a request you've already made in your browser -- free, already installed, and often the fastest way to check one page you're looking at anyway. It does not tell you what those headers mean together: whether a Vary: * silently makes the whole response uncacheable, or whether a Cache-Control: public alongside a Set-Cookie header is a shared-cache cookie leak waiting to happen. This tool reads the same headers DevTools would show you and names the specific, well-documented pattern -- so you don't have to already know the RFC details to notice the problem.

Why would I need more than DevTools if I already know what to look for?

If you already know every pattern this tool checks -- Vary: *, public plus Set-Cookie, no-store beside a leftover max-age, Expires silently overridden by Cache-Control, a stale Expires, a weak ETag on a range-capable response, a static asset with no caching headers -- DevTools plus your own judgement is enough. This tool exists for the times you don't want to re-derive all seven from memory on every response, or when you want the same checks wired into CI as a non-zero exit code, which DevTools' UI cannot do -- it has no CLI and nothing to script against.

Does this tool see anything DevTools can't?

No -- it sees the same response headers DevTools already shows you, and nothing more. The difference is entirely in the reading: this tool applies the seven named checks every time, the same way, whether you remember them or not, and it can run from a terminal or a CI job where opening a browser and clicking through the Network tab isn't practical.

Is my target URL or its response headers uploaded anywhere?

No. The CLI's request goes directly from your machine to the URL you name, exactly like the request your browser already makes. The browser report viewer only parses JSON you paste into it yourself, locally in your browser -- nothing about the target, the headers, or the report is sent anywhere. The only thing stored is an anonymous local count of which features were used, with no target URLs or header values in it.

Chasing a specific symptom instead? Why isn't my CDN caching this? walks the six response-header reasons in the order worth checking them. Prefer a command-line comparison? See this checker vs. curl -I.

Evidence, not a determination. This checks a specific, well-documented set of caching-header patterns from one response. It is not a full caching or performance audit and cannot see a pattern it doesn't check for.

why-isnt-my-cdn-caching-this.html.text:
Why isn't my CDN caching this?

← Back to Cache-Control Checker

A response your CDN stores nothing for is almost always one of six things, and they are worth checking in this order — the first one outranks everything below it, so finding it second wastes the time you spent on the others. Every rule here is a protocol requirement with a citation, not a tuning preference: each one is something a compliant cache must do, which is why changing the CDN's settings will not work around it.

All six read off the response headers the origin actually sent. To see yours: 

node check.mjs https://example.com/your-asset.js --json

…then paste the JSON into the report viewer, which names which of these patterns it found and quotes the header that proves each one. Only point it at a system you own or are authorised to test.

1. Vary: * — never reusable, whatever else you set

RFC 9111 §4.1 states that a Vary field value of * always fails to match. A cache may store the response, but it can never select it for reuse against any later request, however identical. This outranks every other caching header in the response: 

Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000
Vary: *

is never served from cache, by any compliant browser or CDN, ever. It is worth checking first for two reasons: no setting on the CDN side can override it, and it is nearly always accidental — copied from a template, or added defensively against a content-negotiation bug that has since been fixed, and then never removed. If you have one header to look at, look at this one.

2. An accidental Set-Cookie

Most CDNs decline to cache a response carrying Set-Cookie by default, and the reason is sound: storing it would mean handing one visitor's cookie to the next one served from that copy. The usual cause is a session framework configured to start a session on every request, including requests for static assets that nobody intended to make uncacheable.

The inverse case is the dangerous one, and it is the reason this checker rates it a danger rather than a notice. If the response says Cache-Control: public and sets a cookie, it is explicitly inviting every shared cache between the origin and the visitor to store and reuse it. A shared cache that is not specifically configured to strip Set-Cookie on write can then serve one visitor's session cookie to a different visitor. "The CDN won't cache this" is the benign symptom of that pairing; a cache that does cache it is the incident.

3. no-store, private, and no-cache are three different things

These are the most commonly confused directives in HTTP caching, and only two of the three stop a CDN from storing anything:

DirectiveBrowser cacheShared cache / CDN
no-storemust not storemust not store
privatemay storemust not store
no-cachemay store, must revalidate firstmay store, must revalidate first

no-cache is the one that catches people out: it does not mean "do not cache". The CDN still holds the bytes and still answers a revalidation with a 304, so it is still saving origin bandwidth. Concluding that a no-cache response is uncacheable — and then going looking for a CDN bug — is a frequent dead end.

no-store alongside a max-age is a contradiction rather than a compromise: the max-age is dead text, because nothing was stored for it to apply to. This checker reports that pairing as a notice, since it usually means two pieces of configuration are fighting and one of them is silently losing.

4. No explicit freshness lifetime at all

A response with no max-age, no s-maxage and no Expires has no explicit freshness lifetime. RFC 9111 permits a cache to apply a heuristic lifetime in that case, but heuristics differ between implementations and plenty of CDNs default to not caching rather than guessing on your behalf. Relying on that default is relying on undocumented behaviour that can change under you.

The clearest version is a static-asset-shaped path — a content-hashed filename, a .js or .css extension — served with no caching headers whatsoever. That is almost never a decision; it is an origin that was never configured for those paths. A hashed filename is specifically designed to be safe to cache for a year, so a missing header there is pure loss.

5. Expires that is overridden, or already stale on arrival

Two distinct failures share one header. First, if both Expires and Cache-Control: max-age are present, RFC 9111 requires the cache to ignore Expires entirely. A long Expires sitting beside a short max-age does nothing at all — the lifetime you think you granted is not the one in effect. 

Cache-Control: max-age=60
Expires: Thu, 31 Dec 2026 23:59:59 GMT   <-- ignored; the lifetime is 60 seconds

Second, an Expires value at or before the response's own Date header means the response is born already stale. That is usually a hardcoded past date left over from being used as a cache-buster, which then keeps busting long after the reason for it went away.

6. A weak ETag on a range-capable response

This one is not a caching failure and will not show up as a cache miss — it is here because it is the caching-adjacent bug people find last and pay for most. RFC 9110 §13.1.5 requires a strong validator for a conditional range request. A response that advertises Accept-Ranges: bytes but returns a weak ETag: 

Accept-Ranges: bytes
ETag: W/"abc123"

cannot safely support If-Range. A resumed download, or a client fetching segments in parallel, can end up assembling bytes that belong to two different versions of the resource. The symptom is a corrupt large file — not a slow one — which is why it is almost never found by someone investigating a caching problem, and why this tool reports it alongside them.

Reading the answer off one response

Every check above is decidable from a single response's headers, which is what the Cache-Control Checker does: one real GET, then a report naming each pattern it matched and quoting the exact header that proves it. It deliberately does not grade your caching strategy or guess at a target hit rate — those depend on your traffic, not on the protocol — and it does not crawl anything beyond the one URL you name.

Related response-header evidence on the same site: Security Headers checker for Content-Security-Policy and clickjacking headers, and Cookie Security checker for Set-Cookie attribute patterns — a different class of finding than the caching headers here, though step 2 above is where the two overlap.

Evidence, not a determination. The rules above are protocol requirements from RFC 9110 and RFC 9111, but a specific CDN's behaviour is also shaped by its own configuration, which this page cannot see. A response that clears every check here can still be uncached because of a rule set at the edge. Treat this as a diagnostic order for the origin's own headers, not a guarantee about any particular provider.
